html:
The Arthashastra is a Sanskrit handbook on how to run a state: taxes, law, spies, war and foreign policy. Tradition says it was written about 300 BCE by Kautilya, also called Chanakya, minister of Chandragupta Maurya. Most scholars now think it was put together over several centuries and reached its final form between about 100 and 300 CE.

The book is cold and practical. Its subject is artha, worldly success, and its main advice is that the king's own interest is the good of his subjects. It covers:

  • the daily timetable of a king, and how to test ministers with secret agents;
  • state control of mines, forests, liquor, weights and trade;
  • law courts, fines and prisons;
  • the "circle of kings": your neighbour is your enemy, and your neighbour's neighbour is your friend.

The text was lost for centuries. In 1905 the librarian R. Shamasastry found a palm-leaf copy in Mysore and published it in 1909. It is often compared with Machiavelli's Prince, written 1,500 years later, and it is a main source for how the Maurya Empire may have worked.
